lecons.html:
A person can be master of himself, and this should be the first of every person’s goals, particularly the Christian’s. The command addressed to us reads: Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. (Rom 12:21) The goal is clear: that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world, (Phil 2:15)

Being master of yourself requires strength of character, the ability to control yourself so as to act instead of react.

A person’s character is the whole made up of his thought system, his emotions, his attitude, his habits and his capacity for decision. These elements of our being influence one another. To get the upper hand over your character, you must begin by training yourself to manage your emotions.

An emotion is a sudden and intense internal reaction that runs through both our body and our soul. It shows itself through psychological signs (inner tension, agitation) and physical signs (trembling, a faster heartbeat).

Each emotion is triggered by a stimulus — a thought or an internal situation — and a cause that is our own. However, when we are overwhelmed by a strong emotion, it is not solely in response to the present event, but often because that event awakens a past experience that has not been digested. Indeed, our brain records all our reactions and reproduces them automatically in similar situations, sometimes without discernment. This explains why the intensity of an emotion felt at a precise moment can be out of proportion to reality.

Emotion and Feeling: A Fundamental Difference

Emotion is distinguished from feeling by its immediacy and its primitive character. While a feeling is an intellectual construction, evolving over the emotions experienced, an emotion is instinctive, spontaneous and physical. For example, we become aware of a feeling of love through the interpretation of the emotions it arouses — “butterflies in the stomach”, blushing, a faster heartbeat.

Primary and Secondary Emotions

Primary emotions, also called basic emotions, are the first ones we experience from our earliest age. There are six of them: fear, joy, anger, sadness, surprise and disgust. Universal, they are easily identifiable in every individual, regardless of origin.

Secondary emotions, on the other hand, involve a personal interpretation and are influenced by our experience and our judgments. For example, guilt comes from a judgment about oneself.

Positive Emotions: A Real Asset

Some emotions are seen as positive because of their beneficial effects on our well-being and personal development. Among them: gratitude, pride, joy, hope, serenity, curiosity, amusement, admiration, inspiration and love.

Developing these emotions makes us more creative, effective, sociable and resilient. They promote openness to change, flexible decision-making and even better resistance to illness. Cultivating them means enriching our intellectual, social and psychological resources, and laying the foundations for a more fulfilled life.

Negative Emotions: An Essential Function

Some emotions are called negative because of the discomfort they can cause: disappointment, shame, sadness, anguish, jealousy, fear, anger, disgust, guilt and frustration.

However, it is crucial to understand that all emotions have a vital function. They are warning signals that push us to act in the face of life’s events. Anger, for example, often reveals an injustice or a lack of respect, while fear indicates danger, and sadness, a loss.

Adapting to Emotions

When we are faced with a threat, our limbic brain (the seat of emotions) activates an alarm signal, generating physiological reactions. Faced with danger, we instinctively adopt one of three coping strategies: fight, flight or submission.

For example, if we find ourselves facing a roaring tiger, our brain triggers an immediate response: leap to attack, run to protect ourselves, or freeze on the spot. However, malfunctions can occur when this alert system activates wrongly — for example, in the face of a little mouse or a harmless remark from a colleague.

So learning to understand and regulate our emotions is essential in order to make them allies in our daily life.

How to manage your emotions?

To manage emotions, you need to follow these three steps:

  • The first is welcoming the emotion by taking the time to feel it, locate it, name it and accept its message.
  • The second is dissecting this message. If we feel fear, anger or sadness, we must ask what these emotions echo (what danger, what injustice, what loss?…).
  • The third step is to investigate by looking for the trigger of the fear and its original cause.

By following these three steps, you will quickly find that your emotional level drops noticeably. Simply because the emotion will have fulfilled its alert function and you will have understood and heard its message.

Despite the large number of emotions we can name, three seem to be central in the Bible. They are fear, anger and joy.

Fear

The Bible deals with several types of fear. Here are some of them:

  • Fear of man (Luke 12:4-5, Prov 29:25, Heb 13:5-6, Ps 118:6-14)
  • Fear of the enemy (Ps 56:4-5)
  • Fear of failure (Josh 1:9, Isa 41:10)
  • Fear of death (Heb 2:14-15)
  • Fear of misfortune (Job 3:25, Ps 91:10, Prov 3:25-26)
  • Fear of darkness (Ps 27:1, John 8:12)
  • Fear of demonic powers (1 John 4:4, Eph 6:10-12, 1 John 5:18)
  • Fear of the unknown (Rom 8:15)
  • Fear of judgment (2 Cor 5:10, John 5:24)
  • Fear of lacking (Ps 23:1, Phil 4:19)
  • Fear of poverty (Matt 6:31-33)
  • Fear of illness (Exod 15:26, James 5:14-15)
  • Fear of loneliness (Ps 23:4, Ps 27:10, John 16:32, 1 John 4:15)
  • Fear of shame (Isa 54:4, Phil 1:20-21)
  • Fear of spiritual failure (Rom 14:4, Phil 4:13, 2 Tim 1:7)
  • Fear of the future (Jer 29:11)
  • Fear of opposition (Rom 8:31, Matt 10:28)
  • Fear of natural disasters (Ps 46:2-3)
  • Fear of insecurity (Ps 4:8, 91:5)
  • Fear of persecution (Matt 5:10-12, 1 Pet 4:12-14)
  • Fear of losing faith (John 14:1, Luke 22:31-32)

The solution the Bible offers against fear is to deliberately trust in God by leaning on his promises in his Word. The verses given beside each type of fear can help you too. Taking refuge in God against fear is a conscious exercise that we must practice continually. That is why we need to know the Bible and keep reading and meditating on it. At some point, it is fitting to leave Bible study for meditation. You must literally eat the Word. The more it takes shape in you, the more your resistance to every form of fear grows.

Anger

There are only three main types of anger in the Bible.

1. The anger of God

In the Bible, God’s anger is often described as a reaction to humanity’s disobedience or wickedness. For example, in the Old Testament, God is angry with the Israelites for their idolatry and lack of faith. But the way God masters his anger is what should hold our attention. He is slow to anger and, what is more, puts out his anger at his own will. His anger does not respond to stimuli but rather to his own principles and decisions. We are his children and must imitate him.

2. The anger of Jesus

In the New Testament, Jesus is described as having been angry on several occasions, notably when he drove the merchants out of the temple. However, his anger was always motivated by love and justice, and he always acted in a just and merciful way.

3. Human anger

The Bible also mentions human anger, which can be caused by events such as injustice, betrayal or frustration.

It is the latter that interests us. Human anger. According to the Bible, not having control of this emotion is synonymous with a scattered life: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly. (Prov 14:29) The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense. (Prov 19:11) Cease from anger, and forsake wrath. Don’t fret; it leads only to evildoing. (Ps 37:8)

The reasons for human anger can range from legitimate to foolish. But even when human anger is justified, it is a problem. “for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” (James 1:20). So the apostle instructs us: “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” (James 1:19)

According to James, we can control when, where and how we get angry in the same way we can control when, where and how we speak. This is definitely what the Holy Spirit shows by juxtaposing the two following clauses: “slow to speak, slow to anger.” Just as I can choose where to speak, I can do so with anger. For that you must be able to foresee the course of events and position yourself accordingly. The Bible gives advice in this direction: The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out. (Prov 17:14) This is prudence: A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it. (Prov 22:3)

We must master the anger that tears relationships apart and gives access to the devil: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil. (Eph 4:26-27) What the Bible commands is that the human being restrain himself enough not to act on his anger.

Techniques to quickly release your anger

1. Release your anger through breathing

This is ideal for releasing all your tension, and the exercise is even more effective if you visualize the things or people that annoy you.

How: With fists clenched, breathe in while raising your shoulders toward your ears and hold your breath. Then lower them, quickly or slowly, depending on your mood at the moment, and breathe out (hard) while relaxing your shoulders and arms and unclenching your fists, as if you were letting go of all your stress and all your anger. Repeat as many times as necessary.

2. Ask yourself questions that force you to leave the sphere of emotion for reason:

  • Why am I angry?
  • Is it already affecting the tone of my voice or another reaction?
  • What am I going to do to benefit God and myself?

Joy

The Bible presents joy as an essential characteristic of the Christian and even as proof of his salvation. That is why the Bible urges the children of God not to hold back the expression of their joy at all. Of the biblical references that justify what we have just said, the following are only a sample: 2 Cor 13:11, 1 Pet 4:12-14, James 1:2-3, Rom 12:12, Rom 12:15, Phil 1:18, Phil 3:1, Phil 4:4.

Joy is a positive emotion that the Bible urges us to activate constantly. The reason is that the joy of Yahweh is your strength (Neh 8:10).

The key to activating and keeping joy is to think of the fact that you have God on your side, that everything that happens to you is because of him, known to him, and controlled by him. Every time you think of the fact that God himself takes care of you, your stress will go down, and serenity and then joy are activated in your heart. Another way to activate your joy is to think that you have brothers and sisters who truly hold you in esteem. You can think in particular of people very close to you and attentive to you. You will not fail to smile. Think of offering them a gift, or of calling them. All this will activate in you a whole host of positive emotions and mainly love and joy. “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35).

Personality is a set of characteristics that a person has. These influence the way he thinks, his motivations and his behaviors.

It is generally accepted that our personality is defined partly by our genes, and partly by the environment in which we grow (family, interactions, experiences, etc.). So personality is relatively stable and does not change radically with age, because it is, in part, defined by our genes. However, our personality is not completely fixed; even if it does not undergo a metamorphosis, it can evolve. Since part of it is influenced by the environment and experiences, our life experience can have an effect on the evolution of our personality.

It seems important to me to specify here that there is no personality type that is “better” than the others. Each type represents an individual’s cognitive mode of functioning, nothing more. There are good guys and bad guys in each of the types. The jerk, in our eyes, is not necessarily one to our neighbor, and probably even less so to himself!

When you work in a group, at school or at work, it can be very useful to recognize your own strengths and to understand the strengths of others. Likewise, when you work on a project with other members of a group, being able to determine the personality at work of a team member, his character traits, his true temperament, lets you realize that some members of the group are competent and talented in carrying out certain actions. By recognizing these differences, the group will be better able to distribute tasks and work together to achieve its goals.

For example, by identifying the one who has the leader’s personality, the group will be able to move forward more effectively toward its goals. The one who seems to have strong cognitive functions will let the group take shortcuts to solve problems, because he has the ability to quickly pinpoint what is wrong and how to get out of it. And the group member who has stable behavior will be an excellent mediator in case of tensions, quarrels or crises.

A. ESTABLISHING YOUR PROFILE

The character test you will take in class will help you better understand your own personality, whether you are an introvert or an extrovert. Note that we are using here the research of the psychologists Isabel Briggs Myers and Katharine Cook Briggs. It starts from a full exploration of preferences to arrive at strengths and weaknesses, as well as compatibility with other people socially and professionally. However, it is not a tool designed to look for a dysfunction or an anomaly. There is no “normal” and “abnormal” personality; everyone is different!

Extraversion (E) — Introversion (I)

The extraversion-introversion dichotomy describes the way people react and interact with the world around them.

Extraverts are outward-facing. They tend to be action-oriented, to enjoy more frequent social interactions and to feel energized after spending time with other people.

Unlike them, introverts are “inward-facing” and tend to be reflection-oriented. They like to enjoy deep, meaningful social interactions and to feel recharged after spending time alone. Social interactions tend to tire them quickly, especially in the presence of loud, highly extraverted people.

We are all extraverts and introverts to some extent. However, most of us tend to have a preference for one or the other.

Sensing (S) — Intuition (N)

This scale examines the way people gather information about the world around them. As with extraversion and introversion, everyone spends time sensing and intuiting depending on the situation. It is just that people tend to be dominant in one area or the other.

People who prefer sensing tend to pay great attention to reality. In particular to what they can learn through their own senses. They tend to focus on facts and details and like to gain practical experience. People who prefer intuition pay more attention to things like patterns and impressions. They like to think about possibilities, imagine the future and abstract theories.

Thinking (T) — Feeling (F)

This scale focuses on the way people make decisions based on the information they have gathered through their sensing or intuition functions. People who prefer thinking give greater importance to facts and objective data. They tend to be consistent, logical and impersonal when evaluating a decision. People who prefer feeling are more likely to take people and emotions into account when they reach a conclusion.

Judging (J) — Perceiving (P)

The last scale concerns the way people tend to deal with the outside world. People who lean toward judging prefer structure and making firm decisions. On the other hand, people who lean toward perceiving are more open, flexible and adaptable. These two tendencies interact with the other scales. Everyone spends at least some time engaging in extraverted activities. The judging and perceiving scale helps determine whether you behave like an extravert when you face new information (sensing and intuition) or when you make decisions (thinking and feeling).

B. THE 16 PERSONALITY TYPES

Each type is then listed by its four-letter code:

  • ISTJ: The Inspector. Reserved and practical, he tends to be loyal, orderly and traditional.
  • ISTP: The Tinkerer. Very independent, he likes new experiences that let him learn on his own.
  • ISFJ: The Protector. Warm and devoted, he is always ready to protect the people he loves.
  • ISFP: The Artist. Easygoing and flexible, he tends to be reserved and artistic.
  • INFJ: The Advocate. Idealistic, calm and mystical. Yet they are very inspiring, creative, analytical and tireless.
  • INFP: The Mediator. Idealistic and endowed with strong values, he strives to make the world a better place.
  • INTJ: The Architect. Very logical, they are both very creative and analytical. They are strategists, with a plan for everything.
  • INTP: The Thinker. Calm and introverted, they are known for having a rich inner world. They are innovative inventors with an unquenchable thirst for knowledge.
  • ESTP: The Persuader. Shrewd, energetic and very perceptive people, who really enjoy spending time with others, focusing on the present moment and living on the cutting edge.
  • ESTJ: The Director. Confident and rule-oriented, he has high principles and a tendency to take charge. He is an excellent manager, with unequaled efficiency when it comes to managing things, or people.
  • ESFP: The Performer. Extraverted, energetic, enthusiastic and spontaneous, he likes to put himself on stage. With them, you are never bored.
  • ESFJ: The Helper. Extraordinarily caring, sociable, gentle and popular people, always ready to help others. He tends to believe the best of others.
  • ENFP: The Champion. Charismatic, energetic, kind, altruistic and always ready to support a good cause. He likes situations in which he can put his creativity to use.
  • ENFJ: The Giver. Loyal and sensitive, he is known for being understanding and generous.
  • ENTP: The Debater. Very inventive, he likes being surrounded by ideas and tends to launch many projects (but may have trouble finishing them).
  • ENTJ: The Commander. Frank and confident, he is very good at making plans and organizing projects.

Online, you will find more explanations about your personality type after taking the test offered in class. You can also reach out to your trainer or to the administration for help in this area.

That said, we must insist that the personality test and profile do not justify a life that departs from God’s will. The Christian should rather use it as a tool to develop his character consciously and to come closer and closer to the word of God. While personality tests can be useful for understanding myself and others better and thus loving and serving those around me more intelligently, they can never replace the Word of God. Far more than measuring our conduct by comparing it to our results on personality tests, let us make sure we measure ourselves against Scripture. God commands every believer to be patient, to show hospitality, to exhort and to be slow to anger (1 Cor 13; 1 Pet 4:9; Heb 3:13; James 1:19). He does not say to practice hospitality only to extraverts. Just as he does not tell only introverts to be slow to speak.

In Scripture, God unfolds a plan for all-encompassing holiness — for all his people. The biblical command provides a better reference for our hearts and lives than any personality test. For, instead of focusing primarily on what we are, Scripture focuses us on what Christ is. Instead of telling us how we will naturally behave according to our type, Scripture promises us a supernatural strength — the Spirit at work in us gives us the power to act like Jesus Christ.

It is true that the way we live out these commands will differ from one believer to another. But the response to each command should be the same for everyone: obedience full of faith, resting on the help of the Holy Spirit — and not our personality — as our strength. My personality must not excuse my sin. On the contrary, God can use my personality for his glory and for my usefulness in his Kingdom.

Thought is an area that must be mastered to keep a good attitude and display good character. Every moment, an incalculable number of thoughts pass through our mind. Some are good, others are bad. We must have control over this area too. But not by preventing thoughts from being born in our mind. Just like emotions, their arrival is uncontrollable since it depends on more or less external factors. But we must choose what we will dwell on and let the others pass without giving them importance. We must not waste time on bad thoughts at all, not even by fighting them. We must simply stop them and move on to something else. Change the subject. Take the initiative to dwell on something positive, constructive and productive. This is the directive the Bible gives concerning thoughts. Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things. (Phil 4:8)

But beyond constantly sorting the thoughts to use, we need to build a renewed system of thoughts, which alone can help a person overcome the horde of negative thoughts. The Bible urges us to this end: Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. (Rom 12:2) This will be done through constant meditation on the word of God. It will restore our soul and align our way of thinking with the word of God, which in turn will be reflected in the control of our emotions. Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. (James 1:21) Above all, always remember that you have the mind of Christ and declare it constantly. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?” But we have Christ’s mind. (1 Cor 2:16) I have the mind of Christ. A sound mind, a blessed mind, a strong mind, a divine mind.

Another fundamental element of character is habits. This is the toughest point. A habit cannot be controlled. It has to be changed. Habits were acquired by repetition. They must be corrected with the same stick: repetition. To succeed with bad habits, you must replace them with another one. You must avoid the boredom of doing nothing. The steps to overcome a bad habit are:

  • Spot the embarrassing habit and how often it occurs
  • Find something to do in its place (read the Bible instead of masturbating, fold your hands instead of nibbling your fingers)
  • Live this way regularly for a period of 7, 15, 21, 30 days (set the period according to your self-discipline. Going from the smallest to the greatest strengthens your personal discipline with this exercise)

To take on a good habit, the process is practically the same. You must make the decision to live this way for a given period. At 21 days we are more inclined to lock in the habit.

A man of strong character knows how to make decisions in record time. It is better to make bad decisions than to remain undecided. Indecision is definitely a bad decision. To make good decisions, you must take the following three steps into account:

1. Follow the Bible

If the Bible is clear on a subject, do not pray and do not think it over. You already know what to do. (2 Tim 3:16-17)

2. Pray

No need to be long or to seek isolation. Bowing your head on the spot and breathing a prayer is enough. (Papa, I count on you to…) (Neh 2:4-5).

3. Think

Put the facts and information together and decide according to your experience and knowledge. (Prov 16:20). Concerning thinking, you must take the following principles into account:

Principle of Information: What do you know about it? If necessary, quickly gather information. (Prov 13:16, Prov 18:13).

Principle of Selection: What exactly do you want? What will contribute to it best? You must be precise in your goal and not want the whole world at once. (Prov 17:24).

Principle of Evaluation: Ask yourself the following questions: 1) Is it necessary? 2) What will it cost in terms of time, energy, money? 3) Is it worth it? 4) Do I have the means? (Prov 20:25).

Principle of Preparation: Do not ignore problems… Tell yourself that things can go wrong and you will have to suffer losses. Are you ready to face them? Do you have a way to climb back up? (Prov 22:3).

Principle of Confrontation: You may still have fears and doubts. You must brave them, especially if it is fear of a person other than God. (Prov 29:25).

From this level, you can already make your decision. Even if you make a mistake, you did well; it is a courageous mistake. But it will really be hard for you to make mistakes by following these steps. God cannot let you down for all that. If you pray, consult the Word, think following the principles, the light of the Holy Spirit will be available to you for a good decision. All of this can be done in record time.

4. Ask for advice

This is an additional step. It is useful for big decisions where you have time to listen to several opinions and compare them, in relation to your goals and to the Word of God. Talk with several people who have already traveled this kind of road and who are mature enough. Compare the opinions and draw instructions from them (Prov 20:18, Prov 24:6).

lecons.titre: Handling your character from your spirit
lecons.html:
The human being is three-dimensional. Every person is a spirit who has a soul and lives in a body.

Character has to do with the soul. The soul is the point of junction between the spirit (the breath of God) and the body. The soul is none other than the seat of our feelings, our emotions and our temperament. It is in the soul that we have the capacity to be moved, to feel, to think, to reason. It is the manifestation of the psychological side of man. But all this in one way or another involves the spirit and the body. The soul is the property of the spirit; the body is the living envelope.

The spirit of the child of God is born again, purified by the blood of Jesus Christ and sanctified by the presence of the Holy Spirit. The spirit cannot sin. It is born of God. Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God. (1 John 3:9) The soul is in transformation. Its salvation is progressive and assured by the revelation of the Word of God. The more we yield to the revelation of the Word, the more we are transformed by becoming renewed in our mind (soul). This progression must be assured and carried on until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. This transformation (renewal) lets the bad educational copy that the soul has recorded dissolve to make room for the will of God. Meanwhile, the body remains unchanged. It must remain so until Jesus Christ returns to transform us (Phil 3:20-21). Moreover, sin is in the body (Rom 8:3), in the form of passions that wage war against the soul. (1 Pet 2:11).

A human being’s character is largely conditioned by his background and upbringing. Since he was raised by other people, he inherited certain empty ways of living and doing.

Every person has strengths and weaknesses of character. In reality, these weaknesses are characteristics of the person that should not necessarily be called weaknesses. They are traits of his personality that, when misused, appear bad. (For example: impatience is simply the desire to go faster. Etc.).

When these personality traits are corrupted by sin through education systems, information, inner wounds, traditions and bad role models, they become what we see as weaknesses of character. Even strengths of character can be bad instruments if they are controlled by sin.

All this can be changed by the Word of God. Of course, this work of correcting character can truly succeed only in the born-again person. When his spirit is born again and indwelt by the Holy Spirit, the individual’s soul can easily be re-educated by the Word of God to reach its salvation. It is in this sense that the apostle Paul gives us the following exhortation: So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure. Do all things without complaining and arguing, that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world, holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ, that I didn’t run in vain nor labor in vain. (Phil 2:12-16)

The biggest problem affecting a person’s character is found at the level of the body. Fleshly passions wage war against the soul. Indeed, the soul must manifest itself through the body. It must use the five senses to receive information from the physical world and to send it out. Yet sin and its workings continue to pass through these channels. The apostle Paul speaks of a law in the body that fights against the law of the understanding or soul. (Rom 7:22-23). The soul ends up taking what it should not and getting muddled from time to time. So the flesh (the body) must be brought under control. This cannot be done by the soul itself. To dominate the flesh (the body), we must live not only by the education of our understanding but by the spirit. (Gal 5:16, 25). According to Romans 8:1-2, it is the law of the Spirit of life in Jesus Christ that frees us from the law of sin and of death that work in the body. Now this is more active in the children of God who walk according to the Spirit. That is to say, those who draw their energy from the divine strength. That is why the Bible tells us to be strong in the Lord and in his almighty strength. (Eph 6:10). The apostle devoted himself to making this prayer for the Christians of Ephesus when they were still a newborn church. Because without it, all spiritual growth is simply a swelling of the ego through learning principles that are easy to repeat but impossible to live. So, just like the apostle Paul, “For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth, and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” (Eph 3:14-19).

Consider yourself a spirit and speak and act as one:

  • Constantly tell yourself: I am a spirit, I have a soul and I live in a body.
  • Pray constantly in the spirit, so that your spirit is strengthened by the strength of God
  • Constantly repeat this request: Lord, strengthen my inner man even more.
  • Read and declare the Bible aloud and constantly over yourself, to strengthen your soul in submission to the will of God
  • Always obey your spirit instantly.

lecons.titre: My toolbox: 18 exercises by character zone
lecons.html:
For each of the six zones of your character, here are three concrete, immediately applicable exercises. You will choose your exercise for each zone in the Character Zones tab, and you can change it every month.

① EMOTIONS

Welcome → Dissect → Investigate → Respond according to the Word

“So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” — James 1:19

E1 — The Emotions Journal

Each evening, note: (1) What emotion did I feel today? (2) What triggered it? (3) How did I respond to it? (4) How should I have responded according to Phil 4:8? No more than 5 minutes. This is not a diary — it is a diagnostic tool.

Frequency: Every evening for 21 days

E2 — The 60-Second Pause

When a strong emotion rises (anger, fear, intense sadness): STOP. Count slowly to 10. Say softly: “The joy of Yahweh is your strength.” (Neh 8:10). Then identify the emotion before acting. The goal: never react in the heat of the moment to a difficult emotion.

Frequency: Every time an emotion rises

E3 — The Prayer of Emotion

Learn to present your emotions to God like the Psalms do: honestly. Write or say aloud: “Lord, I feel [emotion] because of [situation]. I entrust it to you. You promised [verse]. I choose to lean on you.” Do not suppress them, hand them over to God.

Frequency: At least 3 times a week

② PERSONALITY (MBTI TYPE)

Know yourself in order to serve better — without letting the profile excuse sin

“God can use my personality for his glory and for my usefulness in his Kingdom” — Manual M5

E1 — The Test & Reading Your Profile

Take the MBTI test online (16personalities.com — free). Read the full profile. Identify: (1) 3 strengths to put at the service of others, (2) 2 negative tendencies to watch. Write these 5 points and share them with your partner.

Frequency: Once — then reread at D+30

E2 — The Opposite Exercise

Each week, intentionally practice the opposite of your natural tendency. Example: if introverted → take the initiative for a meaningful conversation. If extraverted → spend 30 minutes alone in silence and reflection. If J (judging) → leave a decision pending for 24 hours. Goal: flexibility in the service of the mission.

Frequency: Once a week

E3 — Reconciling Profile and Word

Choose 2 biblical commands that go against your natural tendency (e.g. if quick-tempered: be gentle / if slow to act: act quickly). Write them down. Declare them every morning. Ask your partner to follow them along with you this month.

Frequency: Declaration every morning

③ THOUGHT

Sort your thoughts — not fight them but replace them

“whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely … think about these things” — Philippians 4:8

E1 — Quarantining Thoughts

As soon as a bad thought arrives: do not fight it (that strengthens it). Simply say: “No.” and move immediately to a thought from Phil 4:8. Have a list of 5 positive thoughts ready (a verse, a project, a loved one, a memory of blessing). Exercise: keep a count over 7 days.

Frequency: In real time, all day long

E2 — The 10-Minute Meditation

Each morning: take a verse, read it slowly 3 times, say it aloud, close your eyes and think about it for 5 minutes, ask yourself: what does this verse mean for my day today? Write one sentence of application. This is not Bible study — it is the renewing of the mind (Rom 12:2).

Frequency: Every morning — 10 min

E3 — The Mental Identity Declaration

Write and memorize: “I have the mind of Christ. A sound mind, a blessed mind, a strong mind, a divine mind.” (cf. 1 Cor 2:16). Say it aloud 3 times every morning. Then add 2 other personal declarations about your areas of mental weakness. Example: “I do not dwell on what is negative.” “My mind is governed by the Spirit.”

Frequency: Every morning — 2 min

④ HABITS

Habits are changed by repetition — with the same stick

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” — Romans 12:2

E1 — The Replacement Plan

Identify ONE bad habit to change this month. Write: (1) The exact habit and its frequency. (2) What triggers it. (3) What I replace it with (a concrete, positive action). (4) The exercise period: 7 days / 15 days / 21 days depending on your discipline. Share with your partner, who will follow the progress.

Frequency: For 21 consecutive days

E2 — The Habit Calendar

Draw a table of 21 boxes (one per day). Check each day the habit was kept. If a day is missed, do not give up — resume the very next day. Show the table to your partner at the end of the month. Visible consistency is more motivating than invisible good intention.

Frequency: Daily check — 1 min

E3 — The Morning Small Victory

Take ONE new good habit to anchor. Start with only 5 minutes (not 30). Examples: read the Bible 5 min / do 5 push-ups / drink a glass of water before coffee / pray before looking at the phone. The goal: create regularity first, increase later. From the smallest to the greatest.

Frequency: Every morning — any length

⑤ DECISION-MAKING

Decide in record time — Bible · Prayer · Thinking

“Indecision is definitely a bad decision” — Manual M5

E1 — The Quick Decision Sheet

For every important decision this month: (1) What does the Bible say on this subject? (2) Have I prayed — even for 30 seconds? (3) What are the facts? (4) What is my precise goal? (5) Are the risks manageable? (6) Whom can I consult? Answer these 6 questions — then decide. Do not wait for absolute certainty.

Frequency: For each important decision

E2 — The 24-Hour Decision

Choose a decision that has been pending for more than a week. Apply the 6 steps above. Give yourself 24 hours maximum to decide. Inform your partner of the decision made. The goal: break the pattern of chronic indecision through a concrete act of courage.

Frequency: Once a week for 4 weeks

E3 — The Council of the Wise

For the month’s big decisions: identify 2 or 3 people who have already gone through this type of situation and who are spiritually mature. Consult them separately. Write down their opinions. Compare them with the Word. Decide. This step is not an escape from responsibility — it is the wisdom of Proverbs 20:18.

Frequency: For each big decision

⑥ HANDLING YOUR CHARACTER THROUGH YOUR SPIRIT

The born-again spirit frees us from the law of sin — live from the inside

“Finally, be strong in the Lord, and in the strength of his might” — Ephesians 6:10

E1 — The Spiritual Identity Declaration

Each morning, say aloud and with conviction: “I am a spirit. I have a soul. I live in a body. My spirit is born of God and cannot sin. (1 John 3:9). The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and of death. (Rom 8:1-2). Lord, strengthen my inner man even more. (Eph 3:16).” Then obey your spirit instantly all day long.

Frequency: Every morning — 3 min

E2 — Praying in the Spirit

Devote 10 minutes a day to praying in tongues (if you have received the baptism of the Holy Spirit) or to interceding with groanings — let the Holy Spirit pray through you (Rom 8:26-27). This is not a performance but an exercise in submitting the soul to the spirit. It strengthens the inner man more than any other exercise.

Frequency: 10 min/day — preferably in the morning

E3 — Instant Obedience

Keep a notebook for 7 days: note each time your spirit (conscience, spiritual intuition, conviction) gives an instruction — and note whether you obeyed or not, and how long afterward. Goal: reduce the delay between the spirit’s instruction and the body’s obedience. The final goal: instant, systematic obedience.

Frequency: Notebook over 7 days — then review

objectifs: You manage your emotions — you act, you no longer react impulsively.
You know your personality type and you use it as a tool, not as an excuse.
You master the flow of your thoughts — you choose what you dwell on.
You have replaced at least one bad habit with a good one.
You make firm and quick decisions without paralysis.

qcm.q: What difference does the manual make between an emotion and a feeling?
c: Emotion is always bad
Emotion is instinctive, spontaneous and physical; feeling is an intellectual construction that evolves over the emotions experienced
Feeling is faster than emotion
There is none

qcm.q: How many primary (basic) emotions are there?
c: Three
Twelve
Six
Four
qcm.e: Fear, joy, anger, sadness, surprise and disgust.

qcm.q: What are the three steps to manage your emotions?
c: Welcome, dissect, investigate
Judge, punish, forgive
Flee, deny, forget
Pray, fast, wait
qcm.e: Welcome the emotion, dissect its message, investigate the trigger and the original cause.

qcm.q: Which emotions seem central in the Bible, according to the manual?
c: Love, hatred and envy
Pride, shame and jealousy
Sadness, surprise and disgust
Fear, anger and joy
qcm.e: The manual deals with them one after another.

qcm.q: What solution does the Bible offer against fear?
c: Never think again about what frightens you
Count on your own strength
Deliberately trust in God by leaning on his promises
Avoid all difficult situations
qcm.e: Taking refuge in God is a conscious and continual exercise: we must read and meditate on the Word until we “eat” it.

qcm.q: What should hold our attention in God’s anger?
c: He gets angry as soon as we disobey him
His anger is calmed only by sacrifices
He never gets angry
He is slow to anger and puts it out at his own will, not according to provocations
qcm.e: God’s anger responds to his principles and decisions, not to stimuli. We are his children and must imitate him.

qcm.q: What is character, according to the manual?
c: Only the temperament inherited from parents
The whole made up of the thought system, emotions, attitude, habits and capacity for decision
The result of a personality test
What we show to others
qcm.e: These elements of our being influence one another.

c: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good
Wait for God to act without doing anything
Repay evil for evil
Avoid all conflicts
qcm.e: This is the starting command of this module.

qcm.q: What does the manual say about personality types?
c: There is no “better” type: each type is a mode of functioning
The type changes every year
Some types are better than others
Only extraverts succeed
qcm.e: Your profile is a development tool, not an excuse for sin.

qcm.q: What should you do about a bad thought, according to the manual?
c: Write it down for an hour
Simply stop it, change the subject and dwell on something positive, constructive and productive
Share it with everyone
Fight it with all your strength
qcm.e: We do not control the arrival of thoughts, but we choose the ones we dwell on.

qcm.q: How do you overcome a bad habit?
c: Ignore it until it leaves
Replace it with a good habit, through repetition
Control it by willpower alone
Fight it every evening by praying longer
qcm.e: A habit is not controlled, it is changed: acquired by repetition, it is corrected by repetition.

qcm.q: If the Bible is clear on a subject of decision, what should you do?
c: Ask the opinion of ten people
Pray for a long time before acting
Do what it says: you already know what to do
Wait for a sign

qcm.q: How does the module describe prayer before a decision?
c: It must last at least an hour
It is useless if you have already thought it over
It does not need to be long: bowing your head and breathing a prayer is enough
It requires a long isolation
qcm.e: Nehemiah 2:4-5: Nehemiah prayed briefly before answering the king.

qcm.q: What does the manual say about indecision?
c: It is a quality of wisdom
It is preferable to a mistake
It protects from failure
Indecision is definitely a bad decision
qcm.e: A man of strong character makes his decisions in record time.

qcm.q: How does the manual describe the human being, and what is character linked to?
c: A spirit that has a soul and lives in a body; character is linked to the soul, which is in transformation
A body and a soul without a spirit
A body that has a soul; character is linked to the body
A soul without a spirit; character is fixed
qcm.e: The spirit born of God cannot sin (1 John 3:9); the soul is renewed by the Word.
